author: Lizzy Nyoike
title: Game day street parking closures raise patient access complications for UMN clinics - The Minnesota Daily
text:
Just hours before the Gophers’ football season kicked off early this September, Katie Edmonston arrived for her medical appointment at the M Health Fairview Clinics and Surgery Center. The nearby street parking she expected to rely on was already blocked off.
Edmonston, who receives care from the clinic relating to a longstanding battle with leukemia, usually uses her handicap parking sign to park at nearby meters without paying. With those spaces unavailable and the walk from a parking ramp too far, she had to pay for valet parking.
Her frustration prompted a TikTok video questioning why parking restrictions begin hours before a kickoff game and how these closures affect patients seeking care nearby.
The University said the meters are covered on game days as part of its plan for traffic to ensure safety and prevent conflicts regarding drivers and pedestrians within campus. Edmonston said she understands the need to manage traffic, but questions how early the restrictions begin.
“The day I posted it was like a 7:00 p.m. game, and my appointment was at 9:00 a.m., and the streets were already blocked off,” Edmonston said. “They were blocked off the whole day before as well.”
Edmonston said she has received care at the University for about four years in treatment for her acute myeloid leukemia diagnosis. She transferred to the clinic and surgery center for a bone marrow transplant, and now receives care for complications following treatment.
Beginning in mid-July of 2026, Edmonston attended daily infusion appointments for three months, including weekends.
Those frequent visits made parking a recurring concern. Edmonston said she typically uses metered parking spots along Fulton and Essex streets because her disability parking credentials allow her to park without paying.
Minneapolis media relations coordinator Allen Henry said motorists with accessible credentials can park at available city meters without paying the fee. However, the University requests a city permit restricting parking on both sides of Fulton Street Southeast, between Oak Street Southeast and Huron Boulevard Southeast, specifically on football game days, according to Henry.
The restrictions add travel lane capacity for cars entering and leaving the area as part of the University’s traffic management plan, he said. Henry said there are no designated accessible parking spots on Fulton Street Southeast; however, all nearby public off-street parking facilities in the area have designated accessible spaces.
Edmonston said an accessible space in a ramp does not necessarily mean she can reach the clinic, though.
“I personally can’t walk far enough from the ramp. I am disabled,” Edmonston said.
On one occasion, Edmonston’s mother took time off of work to accompany her for an appointment and dropped her at the clinic entrance before parking. When they asked the hospital whether parking could be validated, the answer was no, Edmonston said.
The University said patients and visitors attending medical appointments during weekday games are charged a reduced $7 rate at a nearby ramp rather than the full event rate. Fairview also offers valet parking, which patients are encouraged to use when making appointments, according to a statement.
Edmonston said medical bills are already costing her about $800 a month, and repeated parking charges add to the expense on top of receiving treatment.
“I mean, if you’re going there every single day, it adds up,” she said. “I think that it’s something that could be easily changed.”
Neither the University nor the city of Minneapolis specified in their statements when meter parking restrictions begin.
summary: Just hours before the Gophers’ football season kicked off early this September, Katie Edmonston arrived for her medical appointment at the M Health Fairview Clinics and Surgery Center. Her frustration prompted a TikTok video questioning why parking restrictions begin hours before a kickoff game and how these closures affect patients seeking care nearby. The University said the meters are covered on game days as part of its plan for traffic to ensure safety and prevent conflicts regarding drivers and pedestrians within campus.
